latin.404: §. IX. Quicquid verò de Luthero ejusque Sententia fiat, istaque vel eadem, vel diversa, à Cameracensis, æstimetur, nobis sufficit, ad non imputandam Cameracensis opinionem hodiernis Lutheranis, hos eam nolle sibi adscriptam.
latin.405: Utut nulli assequamur, quomodo Lutheri Determinatio Colloquii Marpurgensis, his scil. concepta verbis: (Etsi autem, an verum corpus & Sanguis Christi corporaliter in pane & vino Coenæ Domini præsens sit, hoc tempore non concordavimus &c.) à Corporis Christi præsentia in vel cum pane, corporali, adeoque à subtiliori Consubstantiatione, expediri possit; cum verba ista non præsentiam duntaxat veri Corporis Christi in Coena, sed & modum præsentiæ corporalem, quin corporalem hunc præsentiæ modum, in ipso pane, disertissimè profiteantur. Eoque non possumus non colophonis locô, tribus quod aiunt verbis, innuere, quibus Difficultatibus Corporalem corporis Christi in pane præsentiam, sive soli Crassiori, sive & Subtiliori, saltem Lutheri, Consubstantiationi vindicandam, pressam advertamus.
latin.406: Enimverò Consubstantiatio quæcunque etiam Subtilior, maximè Lutheri recitata modò, subtiliori utut, quin subtilissima, nobis haud invitis, accensenda, adversa conspicitur: (1) Expressis Scripturæ ipsiusque Institutionis Sacræ Coenæ verbis, quibus panis quidem corpus Christi dicitur esse, non autem Corpus Christi pani præsens, minus, pani corporaliter præsens, minimè omnium, in ipso pane, corporaliter præsens esse. Certè Corporalis præsentia corporis Christi in pane, præterquam quòd Localem præsentiam inferit, quatenus Corporalis esse dicitur (Corporalitate cum Localitate, saltem intrinseca, æquè latè patente) & inclusionem dicit, quatenus in pane, licèt & extra eum, Corpus Christi corporaliter præsens perhibetur, & eo ipso panis non est Corpus Christi, quia corpus Christi duntaxat in pane corporaliter præsens existere dicitur.
latin.407: (2) Circumstantiis primæ Institutionis: Corpus enim Christi fuit tum temporis corporaliter ad mensam, seu mensæ corporaliter accubuit, adeoque Corporaliter in pane non fuit. Item, quòd si corpus Christi corporaliter in pane tum fuit, cùm Christus Sacramentum Coenæ instituturus, ipsemet panem cum discipulis edit. Matth. 26. 29. Marc. 14. 25. sequetur, eundem in & sub pane, suam propriam carnem comedisse; adeoque totum suum corpus & animam, tum temporis in ore habuisse: hincque adeo, vel multiplicationem esse factam ejusdem corporis Christi, vel duo Christum habuisse corpora, unum continens & comedens, alterum contentum & comesum.
latin.408: (3) Naturæ omnium Sacramentorum, quorum nullum tale signum est, quod rem signatam, secundum suam essentiam, in sese comprehendat. i. e. corpus Christi corporaliter in se contineat: neque enim Sacramenta definiuntur δοχεῖα latibula & vasa includentia res signatas, uti dolium aut cantharus includit vinum, aut marsupium pecuniam, aut cunæ infantem, quibus similibus nonnulli utuntur, ipse etiam Lutherus in Confessione Majore Tom. 2. Witteb. pag. 185. confer etiam Colloquium Maulbrunense Anno 1564. die 15. April. habitum, p. 108. 109.; Sed definiuntur, juxta Augustinum, esse Signa visibilia invisibilis gratiæ. Signi autem natura non est, corporaliter continere, sed signare & significare. Hinc nec Lutherani audent hactenus dicere: Sanguinem Christi corporaliter in aqua Baptismi præsentem esse, vel in hac corporaliter includi.
latin.409: (4) Naturæ Corporis Christi, quod corporaliter in uno tantum loco est, & uti tempore institutæ Coenæ, ad mensam corporaliter, non autem simul supra mensam, in pane, vel in manibus Christi panem sumentibus & frangentibus, fuit; Ita tempore celebratæ adhuc & celebrandæ Coenæ, corporaliter in cælis est & in cælis manet teste Spir. S. Act. 3, 21. ipsôque Christô, etiam in Institutionis Coenæ verbis Matth. 26, 29. 1. Cor. 11, 26. Quemadmodum verò caro Christi, dum in terra fuit corporaliter, non utique erat in Cœlo; ita nunc quia in cælis est corporaliter, non est utique in terris, ait B. Vigilius Lib. 4. Hinc Lutherus ipse, postremis verbis præfationis suæ in Biblia, sic scribit: Des Hohen Priesters Söhne / Die mit dem täglichen Opfer umgehen / sollten auff uns Christen deuten / die wir für unserm Vater Christo / im Himmel sitzend / hie auff Erden / mit dem Leibe wohnen / und nicht hin Durch sind bey ihm / ohne mit dem Glauben geistlich. Ubi observa Lutherum tria dicere (1) Christum sedere in Cœlo, nos corpore esse in terra. (2) Nos corpore non esse cum Christo. (3) Non aliter, quam spiritualiter & per fidem, nos esse cum Christo.
latin.410: Denique (5) Consubstantiatio adversa est Determinationi tam qualitatis internæ, quàm conditionis externæ corporis Christi, sub qua, in pane, corporaliter præsens, & olim, in prima Institutione fuisse, & modò, in omni cœnæ administratione, adhuc esse, credendum est, puta: Num exinanitum & crucifixum? an verò exaltatum & glorificatum? Num animæ rationali junctum? an verò ab hac anima separatum? Num sanguine turgidum; an verò exsangue? Num uti in pane cum sanguine, ita sanguis in vino cum corpore? Num in utraque Coenæ parte, i. e. specie utraque, tàm panis, quàm vini, totum? an pars totius? Dubio determinationis protinus, nec aliter tamen, terminando, quàm si corpus Christi præsens quidem, non tamen corporaliter, verum supernaturaliter ac spiritualiter duntaxat in Coena præsens, sed non in pane, verùm in anima solius credentis ac vera fide manducantis, confiteamur.

pass_a.404: §. IX. Whatever indeed be made of Luther and his Sentence, and whether that be judged the same as or diverse from the Cambrai [cardinal’s], it suffices for us, toward not imputing the Cambrai opinion to today’s Lutherans, that they are unwilling to have it ascribed to themselves.
pass_a.405: Although we follow none who would free Luther’s Determination of the Marburg Colloquy — conceived in these words: (Although however whether the true body and Blood of Christ be corporally present in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, we have not agreed at this time &c.) — from a corporal presence of Christ’s Body in or with the bread, and so from the subtler Consubstantiation; since those words most expressly confess not only the presence of Christ’s true Body in the Supper, but also a corporal mode of presence, nay this corporal mode of presence in the bread itself. And therefore we cannot but hint, in the place of a colophon, in three words as they say, by what Difficulties we observe pressed the Corporal presence of Christ’s body in the bread to be vindicated for either the Crasser alone or also the Subtler Consubstantiation, at least Luther’s.
pass_a.406: For Consubstantiation of whatever kind, even the Subtler — most of all Luther’s just recited, to be counted by us not unwillingly subtler, nay subtlest — is seen adverse: (1) By the express words of Scripture and of the Institution of the Sacred Supper itself, by which the bread indeed is said to be Christ’s body, but not Christ’s Body present to the bread, less corporally present to the bread, least of all corporally present in the bread itself. Certainly a Corporal presence of Christ’s body in the bread, besides that it imports Local presence insofar as it is called Corporal (Corporality ranging equally wide with Locality, at least intrinsic), also says inclusion, insofar as in the bread, though also outside it, Christ’s Body is alleged corporally present — and by that very fact the bread is not Christ’s Body, because Christ’s body is said only to exist corporally present in the bread.
pass_a.407: (2) By the circumstances of the first Institution: For Christ’s Body was then corporally at the table, or reclined corporally at the table, and so was not Corporally in the bread. Likewise, if Christ’s body was then corporally in the bread when Christ, about to institute the Sacrament of the Supper, Himself ate the bread with the disciples (Matt. 26:29; Mark 14:25), it will follow that the same One in and under the bread ate His own flesh; and so then had His whole body and soul in His mouth: hence either a multiplication of the same body of Christ was done, or Christ had two bodies — one containing and eating, the other contained and eaten.
pass_a.408: (3) By the nature of all Sacraments, none of which is such a sign as comprehends in itself the thing signified according to its essence — i.e. contains Christ’s body corporally in itself: for Sacraments are not defined as δοχεῖα, lurking-places and vessels enclosing the things signified, as a cask or tankard encloses wine, or a purse money, or a cradle an infant — which likenesses some use, Luther himself also in the Greater Confession Tom. 2 Wittenberg p. 185; compare also the Maulbronn Colloquy held 15 April 1564, pp. 108–109; But they are defined, according to Augustine, to be Visible signs of invisible grace. But the nature of a Sign is not to contain corporally, but to signify and mean. Hence neither do Lutherans dare thus far to say: Christ’s Blood is corporally present in baptismal water, or corporally enclosed in it.
pass_a.409: (4) By the nature of Christ’s Body, which is corporally in one place only, and as at the time of the instituted Supper it was corporally at the table, not however at once above the table in the bread, or in Christ’s hands taking and breaking the bread; So at the time of the Supper still celebrated and to be celebrated, it is corporally in the heavens and remains in the heavens, the Holy Spirit witnessing (Acts 3:21) and Christ Himself, even in the Institution words (Matt. 26:29; 1 Cor. 11:26). And just as Christ’s flesh, while it was corporally on earth, was by no means in Heaven; so now because it is corporally in the heavens, it is by no means on earth, says Blessed Vigilius bk. 4. Hence Luther himself, in the last words of his preface to the Bible, writes thus: The High Priest’s sons who deal with the daily sacrifice should point to us Christians, who before our Father Christ sitting in Heaven dwell here on earth with the body, and are not yet through with Him except spiritually by faith. Where observe Luther saying three things: (1) Christ sits in Heaven, we are bodily on earth. (2) We are not bodily with Christ. (3) We are with Christ no otherwise than spiritually and by faith.
pass_a.410: Finally (5) Consubstantiation is adverse to the Determination of both the internal quality and the external condition of Christ’s body, under which it is to be believed corporally present in the bread, and once to have been in the first Institution, and still now to be in every administration of the supper — for example: Whether emptied and crucified? or exalted and glorified? Whether joined to a rational soul? or separated from this soul? Whether swollen with blood? or bloodless? Whether as in the bread with blood, so blood in the wine with body? Whether in each part of the Supper, i.e. each species, both bread and wine, the whole? or a part of the whole? With determination doubtful at once, and yet ending no otherwise than if we confess Christ’s body present indeed, yet not corporally, but only supernaturally and spiritually present in the Supper — not in the bread, but in the soul of the believer alone who eats with true faith.

404: §.IX: whatever one makes of Luther versus Cambrai, today’s Lutherans will not wear Cambrai’s opinion as theirs.
That refusal is enough — we do not impute it to them.
405: Marburg’s determination (we have not agreed whether the true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine) does not free Luther from corporal presence in or with the bread — nor from subtler Consubstantiation.
Those words confess not presence alone but a corporal mode in the bread itself.
Colophon: watch the difficulties that press corporal-in-bread presence for crassior or subtilior (at least Luther’s) Consubstantiation.
406: (1) Scripture and Institution say the bread is Christ’s body — not that the body is present to the bread, less corporally present to it, least of all corporally present in it.
Call presence corporal and you import locality and inclusion; then the bread is not the body, because the body is only said to exist corporally present in the bread.
407: (2) At the first Institution Christ’s body was corporally at the table — so not corporally in the bread.

If it was in the bread while He Himself ate with the disciples (Matt. 26:29; Mark 14:25), He ate His own flesh in and under the bread — whole body and soul in His mouth — hence either multiplication of one body, or two bodies (one eating, one eaten).
408: (3) No sacrament is a sign that contains the thing signified in its essence — sacraments are not δοχεῖα jars enclosing what they signify (cask, purse, cradle), though Luther and Maulbronn use such likenesses.
Augustine: visible signs of invisible grace — a sign signifies; it does not contain corporally.
Hence Lutherans dare not say Christ’s blood is corporally in baptismal water.
409: (4) Christ’s body is corporally in one place only — at the Institution at the table, not also in the bread in His hands; now corporally in heaven (Acts 3:21; Matt. 26:29; 1 Cor. 11:26).
Vigilius: as when on earth it was not in heaven, so now in heaven it is not on earth.
Luther’s Bible preface: we dwell on earth with the body before Christ seated in heaven, and are with Him only spiritually by faith — three points Strimesius marks.
410: (5) Consubstantiation cannot settle the body’s internal quality or external condition if it is corporally in the bread — emptied or exalted? with soul or without? bloody or bloodless? whole in each species or part?
The doubt ends only if we confess the body present in the Supper supernaturally and spiritually — not in the bread, but in the soul of the true-faith eater alone.
